bluf.headline: IV magnesium in acute severe asthma: only uncontrolled reports and one registered trial are available here
bluf.body: The three listed sources are a single case report, a four-patient case series, and a trial registration record. They describe clinicians giving intravenous magnesium to adults with severe acute asthma and reporting improvement, but none of them is a controlled comparison against standard therapy, so they cannot establish whether magnesium changes outcomes.
key_points: A case report describes a dramatic response to IV magnesium in status asthmaticus (REF_1).
A case series of four emergency-department patients given IV magnesium is also available (REF_2).
A trial of IV magnesium in acute asthma is registered as NCT02222222 (REF_3); the record is a registration entry, not a result.
No comparative or controlled data appear in this source set, so no dosing or efficacy conclusion can be drawn from it.
caveats: Case reports and small series are subject to selection and publication bias.
A registry entry describes an intended study; it does not report whether the intervention worked.

content_items.text: A published case report describes a dramatic clinical response to intravenous magnesium in an adult with status asthmaticus.
A case series of four patients given intravenous magnesium in the emergency department adds a small amount of uncontrolled clinical experience.
Neither report includes a comparison group, so improvement cannot be separated from concurrent bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy.
A trial of intravenous magnesium in acute asthma is registered as NCT02222222, indicating the question is being studied formally.
Until comparative results are available, the sources here support only that IV magnesium has been used and observed in severe attacks, not that it should be used routinely.

bluf.headline: No high-tier evidence here: the strongest source is a Tier D case report, so no recommendation on IV magnesium can be supported
bluf.body: Everything in this source set is either one-patient or few-patient experience, or a record that a study has been registered. The highest tier available is Tier D (case report, case series); there is no Tier A, B, or C source. Tier R (registration) contributes no efficacy information at all. All statements below therefore carry LOE III.
key_points: Highest available tier is Tier D - a case report and a four-patient case series.
REF_3 is a Tier R trial REGISTRATION (protocol only, no posted results) and must not be read as evidence that IV magnesium works.
Because only low-tier evidence exists in this set, the honest answer is that usefulness is unproven here.
Any decision to use IV magnesium would have to rest on evidence outside this source set.
caveats: Tier D sources have no control group; apparent responses may reflect co-administered treatment.
Absence of high-tier evidence is not proof of absence of benefit - it is absence of evidence.

sections.title: Highest available evidence (Tier D - case-level only)

content_items.text: The strongest source in this set is a Tier D case report describing a dramatic response to intravenous magnesium in status asthmaticus; a single uncontrolled observation is hypothesis-generating only.
A Tier D case series of four emergency-department patients cannot estimate effect size or support a dose recommendation.

sections.title: What the trial registration does and does not tell us (Tier R)

content_items.text: NCT02222222 is a Tier R record - a trial registration with no posted results - so it establishes only that a study exists, and is not evidence of benefit, harm, or dose.
Stated plainly: within these sources there is no Tier A, B, or C evidence, so no confident recommendation for or against its use is justified.
If a recommendation is needed, retrieval should be extended to randomised trials, meta-analyses, or current guidelines, none of which are present here.

bluf.headline: First-line H pylori treatment in these sources: combination antimicrobial therapy, described most currently by the StatPearls chapter
bluf.body: The available sources are a 1994 review of bismuth-based triple therapy, a StatPearls chapter, and a registration record for a trial of a new quadruple regimen.
key_points: A 1994 review describes bismuth triple therapy (REF_1).
The StatPearls chapter is the broadest source available (REF_2).
A new quadruple regimen is being studied under NCT03333333 (REF_3).
caveats: Antibiotic resistance patterns have changed substantially since the earliest of these sources was written.
None of the listed sources is a current society guideline.

content_items.text: A 1994 review describes bismuth-based triple therapy as an approach to eradicating Helicobacter pylori.
The StatPearls chapter describes eradication as combination antimicrobial therapy with acid suppression.
A new quadruple regimen for H pylori is registered for study as NCT03333333.
The chapter describes confirming eradication after therapy using a non-serological test.
Treatment failure prompts a change of regimen taking prior antibiotic exposure into account.

bluf.headline: Only low-tier sources here: the Tier T textbook chapter is the only usable current synthesis, and the 1994 review must not be read as current practice
bluf.body: The best of these is a textbook chapter, which summarises accepted practice but is not primary research. One source is more than 30 years old. Highest tier available is Tier T; the remaining sources are Tier D (>25 years old) and Tier R (registration, no posted results). No Tier A guideline, meta-analysis, or randomised trial is present.
key_points: Tier T StatPearls chapter is the only source describing contemporary practice.
REF_1 is a Tier D narrative review from 1994, more than 25 years old; treat as historical background, not current first-line guidance.
REF_3 is a Tier R registration with no posted results - it cannot be cited as evidence that the regimen works.
Because only low-tier evidence is available, this describes what a textbook says rather than making a graded recommendation.
caveats: Resistance-driven regimen choice is exactly the point on which a 1994 source is least reliable.
A textbook chapter is not a substitute for a current guideline (Tier A), none of which appears here.

sections.title: Best available source: Tier T textbook synthesis

content_items.text: The StatPearls chapter (Tier T) describes first-line management as multi-drug antimicrobial therapy with acid suppression, selected by local resistance.
The same chapter describes confirming eradication with a non-serological test and selecting a different regimen if treatment fails.
Because this is a textbook synthesis rather than a guideline, it should be checked against a current society guideline before being applied as policy.

sections.title: Historical source - not current practice (Tier D, >25 years old)

content_items.text: A 1994 narrative review (Tier D) describes bismuth-based triple therapy; at over 30 years old it is historical context only and should not be taken as today's first-line regimen.
NCT03333333 is a Tier R trial registration with no posted results; it provides no evidence of efficacy, tolerability, or superiority over existing therapy.

bluf.headline: Sources conflict: guideline and systematic review favour continuing beta-blockade, while one cohort links continuation to worse short-term outcomes
bluf.body: The 2021 ESC guideline advises continuing beta-blockade where haemodynamically tolerated, and a systematic review associates withdrawal with higher mortality. An observational cohort points the other way.
key_points: 2021 ESC guideline: continue beta-blockade where haemodynamically tolerated (REF_1).
Systematic review: withdrawal is associated with higher mortality (REF_3).
An observational cohort reports worse short-term outcomes with continuation (REF_2).
caveats: The cohort finding is observational and may reflect that sicker patients are the ones in whom clinicians continue or stop therapy.

content_items.text: The 2021 ESC heart failure guideline recommends continuing beta-blockade during decompensation where haemodynamically tolerated.
A systematic review found that withdrawal of beta-blocker therapy was associated with higher mortality.
An observational cohort found that beta-blocker continuation was associated with worse short-term outcomes.
Because the cohort is non-randomised, the association may be confounded by the severity of decompensation.

bluf.headline: Two Tier A sources support continuing beta-blockade where haemodynamically tolerated; the opposing signal is a lower-tier Tier C cohort
bluf.body: The strongest sources - a recent guideline and a systematic review - both support continuation where tolerated, because stopping is linked to more deaths. A single observational study disagrees, but that design cannot separate the drug's effect from how sick the patient was. REF_1 (Tier A) and REF_3 (Tier A) concur and carry LOE I; REF_2 (Tier C) carries LOE II and is subject to confounding by indication.
key_points: Tier A guideline: continue beta-blockade where haemodynamically tolerated.
Tier A systematic review: withdrawal is associated with higher mortality - concordant with the guideline.
Tier C cohort associates continuation with worse short-term outcomes; as observational data it does not overturn concordant Tier A evidence.
Continue unless the patient is not haemodynamically tolerating it.
caveats: 'Haemodynamically tolerated' is the operative condition; it does not endorse continuation in shock.
The Tier C cohort is a genuine safety signal worth monitoring - downweighted, not dismissed.

sections.title: Highest-tier evidence (Tier A) - both sources agree

content_items.text: The 2021 ESC guideline is Tier A and recent: continue beta-blockade during decompensation where haemodynamically tolerated.
A Tier A systematic review found withdrawal associated with higher mortality; the two highest-tier sources are concordant.

sections.title: The dissenting source and how much weight it deserves (Tier C)

content_items.text: A Tier C observational cohort reports worse short-term outcomes with continuation; one tier below the concordant Tier A sources, it is not sufficient to reverse the recommendation.
The most likely explanation is confounding by indication, precisely the bias that Tier A designs mitigate.
Weighting by tier: continue beta-blockade when haemodynamics permit, per the Tier A guideline.
Reserve withdrawal for patients not tolerating it, recognising the Tier A review's mortality association.

bluf.headline: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ocular emergency treated by urgent intraocular pressure reduction followed by laser iridotomy
bluf.body: The StatPearls chapter describes it as a sight-threatening emergency. Management is immediate medical lowering of intraocular pressure with urgent ophthalmology involvement, followed by definitive laser peripheral iridotomy.
key_points: Treat as an emergency: urgent ophthalmology referral alongside immediate pressure-lowering therapy.
Laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive treatment.
The fellow eye is at risk and is usually treated prophylactically.
caveats: Systemic agents such as acetazolamide and mannitol have contraindications.
The chapter is a textbook synthesis rather than trial data.

content_items.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma requires immediate intraocular pressure reduction and urgent ophthalmology involvement.
Medical therapy includes topical aqueous-suppressing agents, a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, systemic acetazolamide, and hyperosmotic therapy.
Pilocarpine is used to break the pupillary block once pressure has fallen enough.

sections.title: Definitive treatment and the fellow eye

content_items.text: Laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive treatment, performed once corneal clarity allows.
Prophylactic iridotomy of the fellow eye is described as standard practice.

bluf.headline: Only a Tier T textbook chapter is available: it describes urgent pressure-lowering then laser iridotomy, but this is synthesis, not primary evidence
bluf.body: This answer comes from a single textbook chapter. Textbooks summarise accepted standard care but are not trials or guidelines, so nothing here can be graded as strong evidence. The sole source is Tier T; there is no Tier A guideline, Tier B trial, or Tier C comparative study, so every statement is presented as accepted practice rather than demonstrated efficacy.
key_points: Tier T source only - treat as orienting standard-of-care description, not graded evidence.
The chapter describes an ocular emergency requiring immediate pressure reduction.
Laser peripheral iridotomy is described as definitive, with prophylactic treatment of the fellow eye.
caveats: Stated plainly: with only low-tier (Tier T) evidence available, no comparative claim can be made about which agent or sequence is best.
A current ophthalmology guideline (Tier A) should be sought before this content is used to set protocol.

content_items.text: The only source retrieved is a Tier T textbook chapter - a peer-reviewed synthesis rather than primary research - so management below is reported as conventional care, not an evidence-graded recommendation.
The chapter describes an ophthalmic emergency: intraocular pressure must be lowered immediately and ophthalmology involved urgently.
Medical therapy comprises topical aqueous suppressants, a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, systemic acetazolamide, and hyperosmotic therapy; pilocarpine once pressure falls.

sections.title: Definitive treatment and the fellow eye (Tier T)

content_items.text: Laser peripheral iridotomy is described as the definitive treatment.
Prophylactic iridotomy of the unaffected fellow eye is described; note this is textbook-level (Tier T) guidance, not a trial-supported claim.

bluf.headline: Single IV doses of ondansetron above 16 mg are not recommended because of dose-dependent QT prolongation
bluf.body: The FDA product label sets the dose ceiling: the 32 mg single intravenous dose was withdrawn because of dose-related QT interval prolongation. A case report of torsades de pointes illustrates the arrhythmia risk, and a randomised trial addresses what doses are actually needed.
key_points: Avoid single IV doses above 16 mg in adults (REF_1).
The 32 mg single IV dose was withdrawn for QT prolongation (REF_1).
Torsades de pointes has been reported after high-dose IV ondansetron (REF_2).
Trial data inform the doses actually required for effect (REF_3).
caveats: Risk is higher with electrolyte abnormalities, congenital long QT, and other QT-prolonging drugs.

content_items.text: The FDA product label states that single intravenous doses greater than 16 mg should no longer be used.
The label identifies risk factors including electrolyte abnormalities and congenital long QT syndrome.
A case report documents torsades de pointes following high-dose intravenous ondansetron.
A randomised controlled trial of ondansetron dosing in postoperative nausea provides comparative data on the doses required.

bluf.headline: Tier A regulatory label sets the ceiling: no single IV dose above 16 mg; the 32 mg single dose was withdrawn for QT prolongation
bluf.body: The drug's official label is the authoritative source here. A randomised trial supports what doses are actually needed, and a single case report is consistent with the warning but is not itself the reason for the limit. REF_1 is Tier A and REF_3 is Tier B, both LOE I; REF_2 is Tier D, LOE III, hypothesis-supporting only.
key_points: Tier A label: single IV doses >16 mg are not recommended; the 32 mg dose was withdrawn for dose-dependent QT prolongation.
Tier A label flags the risk modifiers - electrolyte abnormality, congenital long QT, concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.
Tier B RCT informs the effective dose range, showing the ceiling does not compromise efficacy.
Tier D case report is corroborating but should not be presented as the evidentiary basis for the limit.
caveats: The maximum differs by indication and route; the Tier A label is the reference.
A single Tier D case report cannot quantify risk - it establishes that the harm can occur, not how often.

sections.title: Highest-tier source: the regulatory label (Tier A)

content_items.text: The FDA product label - Tier A regulatory evidence - states that single intravenous doses greater than 16 mg should no longer be used, the 32 mg dose having been withdrawn for dose-dependent QT prolongation.
The same Tier A source specifies the populations in whom QT risk is amplified, where ECG and electrolyte monitoring is warranted.

sections.title: Trial evidence on dose requirements (Tier B)

content_items.text: A recent randomised controlled trial (Tier B) provides comparative data on doses needed for antiemetic effect, supporting that control is achievable within the label's ceiling.

A Tier D case report describes torsades de pointes after high-dose intravenous ondansetron; consistent with the Tier A warning but on its own cannot establish incidence and must not be weighted as trial or regulatory evidence.
